subject: Science
title: Asha's Quest: What is Science?
hook: A curious girl discovers that science is all around her—in the kitchen, the garden, and everywhere she looks.

characters.name: Asha
characters.role: curious student exploring the world

characters.name: Grandpa
characters.role: wise village elder who teaches through observation

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Asha's friend who likes to experiment

slides.title: The Wonderful World of Science
slides.storyContext: Asha sits in her grandmother's kitchen watching dough rise, and asks: 'What makes bread puff up?' Her grandfather smiles and says, 'That's science!'

slides.title: Asha's Discovery Begins
slides.storyContext: Asha notices that yeast in warm water makes the dough rise, that salt dissolves in her soup, and that her reflection appears in water. She asks herself: 'How does everything around me work?' This is how science begins—with curiosity and questions.
slides.inSimpleWords: Science starts when you ask questions about things you see every day.

image.alt: Asha's Discovery Begins — The Wonderful World of Science

slides.title: What is Science?

points.text: Science is a way of asking questions and finding answers using careful observation and experiments.
Scientists observe nature, ask 'why' and 'how', and then test their ideas to find the truth.
Science is not just in laboratories—it is in your kitchen, garden, and playground.

slides.inSimpleWords: Science is asking questions about the world and finding answers through testing and watching.

image.alt: What is Science? — The Wonderful World of Science

slides.title: Branches of Science

points.label: Physics
points.text: Studying motion, light, heat, and how things move (why a ball falls, how a fan works).

points.label: Chemistry
points.text: Studying materials and how they change (how milk becomes curd, how wood burns).

points.label: Biology
points.text: Studying living things—plants, animals, and how they grow and survive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Science has three main branches: physics (how things move), chemistry (what things are made of), and biology (how living things work).

slides.title: The Scientific Method

points.text: Observe: Watch something carefully in nature or in an experiment.
Question: Ask 'why' or 'how' does this happen?
Hypothesize: Make a guess about what might happen.
Experiment: Test your guess carefully.
Conclude: See if your guess was right.

example.problem: Ravi wonders: Does a heavier ball fall faster than a light ball? What should he do?
example.solution: Observe: He watches objects falling. Question: Do heavy and light objects fall at different speeds? Hypothesis: Heavier things fall faster. Experiment: Drop a heavy stone and a light feather from the same height. Conclude: In air, the feather floats down slowly because air resistance pushes it up, but in a vacuum they fall at the same speed.

slides.inSimpleWords: The scientific method is: observe, question, guess, test, and see if you were right.

image.alt: The Scientific Method — The Wonderful World of Science

slides.title: Science in Daily Life

points.text: Cooking: heating, mixing, fermentation (yeast, curd)
Farming: understanding soil, water, sunlight, and seasons
Medicine: antibiotics, vaccines, bandages
Technology: smartphones, fans, lights, vehicles

example.problem: Asha's mother cooks rice. What science is happening?
example.solution: Heat energy makes water boil. Starch in rice absorbs the hot water and swells. When cooled, the rice becomes soft and edible. This is physics (heat), chemistry (starch changing), and biology (nutrients for our body).

slides.inSimpleWords: Every day you use science: cooking, farming, staying healthy, and using machines.

image.alt: Science in Daily Life — The Wonderful World of Science

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Science is asking questions and finding answers through observation and testing.
Science has three branches: physics, chemistry, and biology.
The scientific method helps us solve problems step by step.
Science is everywhere in your daily life—cooking, farming, medicine, and technology.

slides.inSimpleWords: Science is the art of asking 'why' and finding answers by watching and testing. It is all around you!

image.alt: What We Learned — The Wonderful World of Science

slides.title: Your Turn: Find Science at Home
slides.storyContext: Asha challenges you: This week, find three examples of science in your home or school. It could be something that heats, changes color, grows, or moves. Write down what science is happening.

example.problem: I see milk turning into curd in the kitchen. What science is this?
example.solution: This is chemistry and biology. Bacteria in the yogurt starter (or naturally present) eat the lactose in milk and produce acid. The acid makes the milk protein coagulate (clump together), turning it into curd.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around you! Science is happening in your kitchen, garden, and everywhere.

subject: Science
title: Ravi's Wildlife Adventure: The Amazing Variety of Life
hook: A village boy discovers that living things come in endless shapes, sizes, and ways of life—from tiny insects to giant trees.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: curious naturalist exploring the village and forest

characters.name: Maya
characters.role: Ravi's sister who loves collecting leaves and insects

characters.name: Forest Guard Dada
characters.role: local expert who teaches about wildlife

slides.title: Diversity in the Living World
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Maya explore their village and nearby forest, spotting insects, birds, plants, fish, and creatures they've never seen before. Forest Guard Dada says, 'Each living thing has a different way of surviving!'

image.alt: Diversity in the Living World — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Life in the Village and Forest
slides.storyContext: Ravi finds an ant carrying a grain of rice. Maya sees a butterfly on a flower. They spot a fish in the pond, a frog jumping, a bird building a nest, and a tree growing taller every year. 'How are they all so different?' Ravi asks. 'Because each one is perfectly designed for where it lives,' Dada replies.
slides.inSimpleWords: Living things are different because they live in different places and have different ways of surviving.

image.alt: Life in the Village and Forest — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What is Biodiversity?

points.text: Biodiversity means the variety of all living things on Earth—animals, plants, insects, fish, fungi, and microorganisms.
No two living things are exactly the same. Each has special features that help it survive.
India is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world—we have jungles, grasslands, deserts, mountains, and coasts.

example.problem: Why does a fish have fins but a bird has wings?
example.solution: Both fish and birds move through their environments, but fish move through water and birds move through air. Fins help fish swim, and wings help birds fly. Each body part is designed for that animal's lifestyle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Biodiversity is all the different living things in the world, and each one is special in its own way.

slides.title: Classification of Living Things

points.label: Animals
points.text: They eat food (cannot make their own). Insects, fish, frogs, birds, snakes, cows, tigers.

points.label: Plants
points.text: They make food using sunlight. Trees, grass, flowers, vegetables.

points.label: Microorganisms
points.text: Tiny living things we cannot see without a microscope: bacteria, fungi, amoeba.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things are sorted into groups: animals that eat, plants that make their own food, and tiny creatures we cannot see.

slides.title: Adaptation: Living in Your Environment

points.label: Desert animals
points.text: Camel stores water in its hump; snake hides underground; lizard is fast and has light color.

points.label: Forest animals
points.text: Monkey swings on trees; snake blends with leaves; tiger is strong.

points.label: Water animals
points.text: Fish has gills to breathe water; frog has webbed feet; duck has waterproof feathers.

example.problem: Why does a snake have no legs but can move very fast on the ground?
example.solution: A snake's long, flexible body and strong muscles allow it to move by sliding and coiling. Its scales reduce friction with the ground. This adaptation is perfect for hunting in grass and hiding in small spaces.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every animal has special features that help it survive where it lives.

image.alt: Adaptation: Living in Your Environment — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Human Diversity

points.text: Humans come in different heights, skin colors, hair colors, and builds.
These differences are due to genes passed down from parents and adaptation to different climates.
Despite differences, all humans are one species and deserve equal respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: People look different, but we are all human and special in our own way.

image.alt: Human Diversity — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: A Day in Ravi's Forest Adventure
slides.storyContext: Ravi spends a morning in the forest near the village. He counts different animals he sees.

example.problem: Ravi spots: 3 ants, 5 butterflies, 2 birds, 1 snake, 4 grasshoppers, 1 tree with holes from woodpeckers, and 2 different kinds of flowers. How many living things did he observe? Name the groups they belong to.
example.solution: Total living things: 3+5+2+1+4+1+2 = 18. Groups: Insects (ants, butterflies, grasshoppers, woodpeckers = 3 types), other animals (bird, snake = 2 types), and plants (tree, flowers = 2 types). This shows biodiversity!

slides.inSimpleWords: Every time you look carefully at nature, you see the amazing variety of life.

image.alt: A Day in Ravi's Forest Adventure — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things on Earth.
Living things are grouped into animals, plants, and microorganisms.
Each animal has special adaptations to survive in its environment.
Humans also have diversity, and all humans deserve respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: The world is full of different living things, and each one is specially designed for where it lives.

image.alt: What We Learned — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Your Turn: Observe Biodiversity Around You
slides.storyContext: Go to a park, garden, or forest near you. Spend 15 minutes observing. Count how many different animals and plants you can find. List them by group (insects, birds, reptiles, plants, etc.).

example.problem: You find a mosquito, a butterfly, a dog, and a mango tree. Sort them into groups.
example.solution: Insects: mosquito, butterfly. Animals (mammals): dog. Plants: mango tree. This shows biodiversity in even a small area!

slides.inSimpleWords: Take time to look at nature carefully. You will be amazed at the variety of life around you.

image.alt: Your Turn: Observe Biodiversity Around You — Diversity in the Living World

subject: Science
chapter: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
title: Priya's Kitchen Quest: The Secret of Good Food
hook: A girl learns that eating the right food keeps her body strong, active, and healthy—and that different foods do different jobs.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: health-conscious student learning about nutrition

characters.name: Mother
characters.role: caring parent who cooks nutritious meals

characters.name: School Nurse Aunty
characters.role: health educator who teaches about nutrition

slides.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
slides.storyContext: Priya feels tired during sports class. Her mother says, 'You need to eat balanced food to stay strong.' Priya learns that food is fuel and medicine for the body.

image.alt: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body — Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

slides.title: Food Powers the Body
slides.storyContext: Priya's school nurse explains: when you eat, your body breaks food down into tiny pieces. These pieces become energy for running, thinking, and growing. Some foods build muscles, some give energy, and some keep your body working smoothly. Priya realizes: 'I am what I eat!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Food gives your body energy, helps it grow, and keeps it healthy.

slides.title: Nutrients: What Your Body Needs

points.label: Carbohydrates
points.text: Rice, wheat, potatoes, sugar. They give energy for running, playing, and thinking.

points.label: Proteins
points.text: Milk, eggs, dal, meat, fish, nuts. They build muscles and repair the body.

points.label: Fats
points.text: Oil, butter, nuts, seeds. They store energy and protect organs.

points.label: Vitamins & Minerals
points.text: Fruits, vegetables, milk. They keep bones strong and fight disease.

points.label: Water
points.text: Most important! It dissolves nutrients and keeps every cell alive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body needs five types of food: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth), fats (storage), vitamins (health), and water (life).

slides.title: Balanced Diet: The Magic Mix

points.text: A balanced diet has the right amount of each nutrient.
Half your plate should be vegetables and fruits; one quarter grain/carbs; one quarter protein.
Eating different colored foods ensures you get different vitamins: orange (vitamin A), red (lycopene), green (minerals).

example.problem: Priya's lunch is only rice and salt. Is it balanced?
example.solution: No. It has carbs but no protein, fat, vitamins, or minerals. A balanced lunch would be: rice (carbs) + dal (protein) + ghee (fat) + vegetables (vitamins/minerals) + water. This gives her body everything it needs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat different kinds of food to give your body everything it needs.

slides.title: Common Foods in India and Their Nutrients

points.label: Rice & Wheat
points.text: Carbohydrates = energy

points.label: Dal (Lentils)
points.text: Proteins = muscle building

points.label: Milk & Yogurt
points.text: Calcium = strong bones and teeth

points.label: Vegetables (leafy greens, carrots, tomatoes)
points.text: Vitamins & minerals = healthy body

points.label: Ghee & Oil
points.text: Fats = energy storage

points.label: Fruits (mango, banana, orange, guava)
points.text: Vitamins & fiber = digestion and immunity

slides.inSimpleWords: Indian foods like rice, dal, milk, vegetables, and fruits have all the nutrients your body needs.

slides.title: Digestion: How Your Body Uses Food

points.text: Mouth: teeth chew food into small pieces; saliva starts breaking it down.
Stomach: strong acids and muscles turn food into a paste.
Small intestine: absorbs nutrients into the blood.
Large intestine: takes back water; leftover waste becomes stool.
This whole journey takes 24-30 hours!

example.problem: You eat a banana. Trace its path through your body.
example.solution: Mouth: teeth break it; saliva mixes in. Stomach: acid and muscles turn it into paste. Small intestine: sugars and minerals enter blood. Large intestine: water is absorbed. Leftover fiber becomes waste. Energy from the banana reaches your cells in 1-2 hours!

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body is smart! It breaks down food and takes out what it needs.

slides.title: Priya Plans Her Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: Priya writes down what she ate in a day and checks if it is balanced.

example.problem: Breakfast: 2 rotis with ghee, milk, banana. Lunch: rice, dal, vegetables, yogurt. Snack: apple, nuts. Dinner: wheat bread, egg curry, spinach, water. Is this balanced?
example.solution: Yes! Breakfast: carbs (rotis) + fat (ghee) + protein & calcium (milk) + vitamins (banana). Lunch: carbs (rice) + protein (dal) + vitamins (vegetables) + calcium (yogurt). This covers all nutrients!

slides.inSimpleWords: Plan your meals to include different food groups each day.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Food gives energy, helps growth, and keeps the body healthy.
Five nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins/minerals, and water.
A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts.
Digestion turns food into energy and waste.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat a variety of healthy foods to keep your body strong and your mind sharp.

image.alt: What We Learned — Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan a Balanced Meal
slides.storyContext: Design a lunch that has carbs, protein, fat, vitamins, and minerals. Use foods from your kitchen.

example.problem: Create a lunch using only dal, rice, oil, and water. How do you make it balanced?
example.solution: Rice (carbs) + dal (protein) + oil/ghee (fat) + water (hydration). Add vegetables or leaves if available for vitamins. This is a simple but complete meal!

slides.inSimpleWords: Think before you eat: Does my meal have energy, growth, and health?

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Magnet Mystery: The Invisible Force
hook: A curious boy discovers that magnets have an invisible power that can pick up metal from far away—and the Earth itself is a giant magnet!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: inquisitive student experimenting with magnets

characters.name: Sister Divya
characters.role: helps with experiments and takes notes

characters.name: Physics Teacher
characters.role: explains magnetic science

slides.title: Exploring Magnets
slides.storyContext: Arjun's toy train has a magnet underneath. When he holds it near metal scraps, they jump up! 'How does it pull from distance?' he asks. His teacher smiles: 'That is magnetism!'

slides.title: The Magnet's Invisible Pull
slides.storyContext: Arjun collects iron nails, paper clips, and coins. He brings a magnet near them one by one. The nails and clips jump to the magnet, but the coin doesn't move. 'Some things are magnetic, some are not!' he realizes. He learns that magnets create an invisible force field around them.
slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet has an invisible power that pulls certain metals toward it.

slides.title: What is a Magnet?

points.text: A magnet is an object that produces a force field, invisible to the eye.
This force field attracts (pulls) metals that contain iron.
The force works through air, water, and paper—it does not need to touch!
Every magnet has two poles: North and South.

example.problem: Arjun holds a magnet above a glass of water with paper clips inside. Do the paper clips move to the magnet?
example.solution: Yes! The magnetic force passes through the glass and water. The paper clips are pulled up. This shows that magnetic force does not need physical contact.

slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet is a thing that pulls metals from a distance using an invisible force.

slides.title: Magnetic Poles and Forces

points.label: North Pole
points.text: The end of a magnet that points north when it hangs freely.

points.label: South Pole
points.text: The end of a magnet that points south when it hangs freely.

points.label: Like poles repel
points.text: North to North or South to South push away from each other.

points.label: Opposite poles attract
points.text: North to South pull toward each other.

example.problem: Arjun has two bar magnets. When he brings them close, they spin to face each other. Why?
example.solution: If North poles face each other, they repel (push away). If North faces South, they attract (pull together). The magnets are naturally finding the position of strongest pull or push.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets can push each other away (repel) or pull each other (attract) depending on which poles face each other.

slides.title: Types of Magnets

points.label: Bar magnet
points.text: A rectangular or cylindrical magnet, strongest at the poles.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: A magnet made by wrapping wire around iron and running electric current through it. Stronger than bar magnets!

points.label: Temporary magnet
points.text: A piece of iron that becomes magnetic when touched by a real magnet, but loses power when removed.

points.label: Permanent magnet
points.text: Always magnetic (like bar magnets); never loses its power.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some magnets are natural and always work. Others are made by electricity and can be turned on or off.

slides.title: Earth is a Magnet!

points.text: The Earth has a magnetic field caused by molten iron in its core.
This is why a compass needle always points North—it aligns with Earth's field.
The North Pole of a compass points toward geographic North.
Migrating birds and whales use Earth's magnetic field to navigate.

example.problem: A compass is placed on a table in different positions. Why does the needle always point the same direction?
example.solution: The compass needle is a tiny magnet. Earth's magnetic field pulls its North pole toward geographic North. No matter how you rotate the compass, the needle realigns itself.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is like a giant magnet. That's why compasses point north!

image.alt: Earth is a Magnet! — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Arjun's Magnet Experiments
slides.storyContext: Arjun conducts three simple experiments in his room.

example.problem: Experiment 1: A magnet is held above paper clips on a table. How many can it pick up? Experiment 2: A magnet is wrapped in plastic and held above coins. What happens? Experiment 3: A magnet is placed inside a closed jar with paper clips in water. Can it still attract them?
example.solution: 1. It picks up 20-30 clips (depends on magnet strength). 2. Coins are not magnetic, so nothing happens. 3. Yes, the magnetic force passes through plastic, glass, and water. Magnetic force is invisible and very powerful!

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets work through materials; their invisible force is everywhere around them.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A magnet is an object with an invisible force field that attracts iron.
Every magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
Like poles repel; opposite poles attract.
Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are amazing! They pull metals without touching and even guide our navigation.

image.alt: What We Learned — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Your Turn: Explore Magnetism
slides.storyContext: Take a magnet and a collection of items (nails, coins, paper, plastic, aluminum foil, rubber, wood). Test each item. Which are magnetic? Can you find anything not magnetic?

example.problem: You test 10 items with a magnet. Nails, paper clips, bolts, and screws stick. Coins, rubber, plastic, wood, and paper do not. What can you conclude?
example.solution: Magnetic items contain iron. Non-magnetic items do not. Only iron-based metals are attracted to magnets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not everything is magnetic! Only iron and some other metals stick to magnets.

subject: Science
title: Vikram's Racing Challenge: How Far? How Fast?
hook: A village boy learns to measure distance and speed using standard units—and discovers that motion is all around him.

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: athletic student interested in racing and speed

characters.name: Cousin Pooja
characters.role: helps measure and keep track

characters.name: Coach Uncle
characters.role: village sports trainer who teaches measurement

slides.title: Measurement of Length and Motion
slides.storyContext: Vikram and friends hold a village race. But when they argue about who ran the farthest, they realize they need a proper way to measure. Coach Uncle arrives with a measuring tape: 'Let's use standard units!'

image.alt: Measurement of Length and Motion — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Why Measurement Matters
slides.storyContext: Vikram says, 'I ran far!' His friend says, 'No, I ran farther!' But they have no proof. Coach Uncle explains: 'In science, we cannot use words like far or fast. We need to measure with numbers and standard units. That's why the world agreed on meters and seconds.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We need standard units to measure so everyone understands the same thing.

slides.title: Standard Units of Length

points.label: Millimeter (mm)
points.text: Smallest, used for tiny things like the thickness of a book.

points.label: Centimeter (cm)
points.text: Used for small objects: pencil length, hand width.

points.label: Meter (m)
points.text: Used for rooms, height, distance in a field.

points.label: Kilometer (km)
points.text: Used for long distances: between villages, cities.

example.problem: Vikram measures his room: 4 meters long, 3 meters wide. What is the perimeter?
example.solution: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2(4 + 3) = 2 × 7 = 14 meters. A rope around the room would be 14 meters long.

slides.inSimpleWords: We measure length in millimeters (tiny), centimeters (small), meters (big), and kilometers (very big).

slides.title: Measuring Length: Tools and Methods

points.label: Ruler/Scale
points.text: For small objects; accurate up to 1 mm.

points.label: Measuring tape
points.text: For longer distances and curves; flexible.

points.label: Meter stick
points.text: Exactly 1 meter; good for rooms and height.

points.label: Odometer in a car
points.text: Measures distance traveled; useful for long journeys.

example.problem: Pooja measures a cricket field from one end to the other. She uses a measuring tape and gets 88 meters. Is this reasonable?
example.solution: Yes! A cricket pitch is 22 yards (about 20 meters) long. But she measured the entire field including boundaries, so 88 meters is reasonable for a full cricket ground.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different tools measure different lengths: rulers for small things, measuring tapes for medium distances, and odometers for travel.

image.alt: Measuring Length: Tools and Methods — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: What is Motion?

points.text: Motion is when something changes position—it moves from one place to another.
Motion requires a reference point. Vikram is running; relative to the ground, he is moving. Relative to himself, he is standing still!
Speed tells how fast something moves: distance ÷ time.
Velocity tells speed AND direction (e.g., 10 m/s north).

example.problem: A car travels 100 kilometers in 2 hours. What is its speed?
example.solution: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 km ÷ 2 hours = 50 km/hour. The car moves 50 kilometers every hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is moving from one place to another. Speed is how fast you move.

image.alt: What is Motion? — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Measuring Speed

points.label: Time needed
points.text: Use a clock or stopwatch; measure in seconds, minutes, or hours.

points.label: Distance covered
points.text: Use a measuring tape or odometer; measure in meters or kilometers.

points.label: Speed formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time

points.label: Units
points.text: m/s (meters per second) or km/h (kilometers per hour)

example.problem: Vikram runs 100 meters in 20 seconds. What is his speed?
example.solution: Speed = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s. Vikram runs 5 meters every second. If he kept this speed for 1 hour (3,600 seconds), he would cover 5 × 3,600 = 18,000 meters = 18 km!

slides.inSimpleWords: To find speed, divide the distance by the time. A fast runner covers more distance in less time.

image.alt: Measuring Speed — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: The Village Race Results
slides.storyContext: Coach Uncle organizes a race with five participants. They run 200 meters each, and he measures their times.

example.problem: Vikram: 200 m in 40 s. Pooja: 200 m in 50 s. Ravi: 200 m in 35 s. Aisha: 200 m in 45 s. Karan: 200 m in 38 s. Who is the fastest? What are their speeds?
example.solution: Speeds: Vikram = 200/40 = 5 m/s. Pooja = 200/50 = 4 m/s. Ravi = 200/35 ≈ 5.7 m/s (fastest!). Aisha = 200/45 ≈ 4.4 m/s. Karan = 200/38 ≈ 5.3 m/s. Ravi is the fastest runner!

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure distance and time to find who is fastest. Speed shows the winner clearly.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Standard units: mm, cm, m, km for length; seconds, hours for time.
Use rulers, measuring tapes, and meter sticks to measure length.
Motion is change of position relative to a reference point.
Speed = Distance ÷ Time. Measured in m/s or km/h.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure length with standard units. Find speed by dividing distance by time. This is how science proves what's fast and far!

slides.title: Your Turn: Measure Speed at Home
slides.storyContext: Measure your own speed. Walk or run a known distance (like 100 meters in your school field or along a road). Use a stopwatch or phone timer. Calculate your speed.

example.problem: You walk 100 meters in 100 seconds. What is your walking speed? If you walked for 1 hour at this speed, how far would you go?
example.solution: Speed = 100 m ÷ 100 s = 1 m/s. In 1 hour (3,600 seconds), you cover 1 × 3,600 = 3,600 m = 3.6 km. That's typical walking speed!

slides.inSimpleWords: Try it yourself! Measure your walking or running speed. You are a scientist!

subject: Science
title: Neha's Material Detective Game: What Is Everything Made Of?
hook: A curious girl discovers that every object is made of different materials with special properties—and learns why we choose certain materials for certain jobs.

characters.name: Neha
characters.role: observant student exploring everyday materials

characters.name: Grandfather
characters.role: elderly craftsman who has worked with many materials

characters.name: Science Teacher
characters.role: explains properties of materials

slides.title: Materials Around Us
slides.storyContext: Neha sits at home and looks around: wood chairs, glass windows, metal spoons, cloth clothes, plastic bottles. 'Everything is made of something different!' she realizes. Her grandfather smiles: 'Each material was chosen because it has special powers.'

slides.title: Why Different Materials?
slides.storyContext: Neha asks grandfather: 'Why is a pot made of metal, not glass? Why are clothes made of cloth, not plastic?' He explains: 'Because each material has different properties. Metal heats quickly for cooking. Glass is clear for windows. Cloth is soft and lets skin breathe. Plastic doesn't break easily. Humans choose the right material for the job.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Different materials are used for different things because each has different properties.

slides.title: What is a Material?

points.text: A material is any substance used to make objects.
Materials come from nature (wood, stone, cotton, metal) or are made by humans (plastic, glass, cement).
Each material has special properties that make it useful for certain jobs.
Properties are the characteristics of a material: color, hardness, flexibility, ability to float, etc.

example.problem: Why is a bridge made of steel and concrete, not plastic?
example.solution: Steel is very strong and hard—it can hold heavy weight. Concrete is also strong and durable. Plastic would break under heavy traffic and weather. The bridge builders chose materials that can last for years under stress.

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials have different properties. We choose the right material based on what the object needs to do.

image.alt: What is a Material? — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Common Materials and Their Properties

points.label: Wood
points.text: Hard, strong, can burn, floats in water, absorbs water slowly. Used for: furniture, boats, houses.

points.label: Metal (iron, aluminum, copper)
points.text: Hard, strong, shiny, conducts heat and electricity, rusts if exposed to water. Used for: pots, tools, wires, structures.

points.label: Glass
points.text: Hard, brittle (breaks easily), transparent, doesn't conduct electricity. Used for: windows, bottles, bulbs.

points.label: Plastic
points.text: Lightweight, flexible, waterproof, doesn't rot, takes 100+ years to decompose. Used for: bags, bottles, toys.

points.label: Cloth (cotton, silk)
points.text: Soft, flexible, absorbs water, breathable, can tear. Used for: clothes, bags, curtains.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each material has a different look, feel, and ability. That's why we use them for different things.

slides.title: Properties of Materials

points.label: Hardness
points.text: How resistant to scratching or denting. Diamond is hardest; clay is soft.

points.label: Flexibility
points.text: Can it bend without breaking? Cloth is flexible; glass is rigid.

points.label: Transparency
points.text: Can light pass through? Glass is transparent; wood is opaque.

points.label: Solubility
points.text: Can it dissolve in water? Salt dissolves; plastic doesn't.

points.label: Conductivity
points.text: Does it conduct heat or electricity? Metal does; plastic doesn't.

points.label: Density
points.text: Is it heavy or light? Wood floats; stone sinks.

example.problem: Why are electrical wires made of copper wrapped in plastic?
example.solution: Copper conducts electricity well—it carries the current. Plastic doesn't conduct electricity—it protects us from getting shocked. Together, they are the perfect combination!

slides.inSimpleWords: Each property of a material makes it good for certain jobs.

slides.title: Natural vs. Synthetic Materials

points.label: Natural materials
points.text: Come from nature without much processing: wood, stone, cotton, leather, wool, silk, clay.

points.label: Synthetic materials
points.text: Made by humans from chemicals in laboratories: plastic, glass, cement, rubber, nylon.
Natural materials are often biodegradable (break down in nature). Synthetic materials often persist (stay for years).

example.problem: A paper bag and a plastic bag. Which breaks down faster in nature?
example.solution: Paper is made from wood (natural). It rots in weeks to months. Plastic is synthetic. It takes 100-1000 years to decompose. That's why plastic bags harm the environment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Natural materials come from nature and rot away. Synthetic materials are made by humans and last a very long time.

slides.title: Neha's Material Hunt
slides.storyContext: Neha examines 10 objects in her home and identifies their materials and properties.

example.problem: Neha finds: 1) wooden chair (hard, natural, floats); 2) glass cup (transparent, brittle, natural); 3) metal spoon (shiny, conducts heat, natural); 4) plastic bottle (lightweight, flexible, synthetic); 5) cotton cloth (soft, absorbs water, natural). Which objects are natural? Which are synthetic?
example.solution: Natural: wooden chair, glass cup, metal spoon, cotton cloth (4 objects). Synthetic: plastic bottle (1 object). Most are natural! But plastic is becoming more common.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around you. Most things are made from a mix of natural and synthetic materials.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Materials are substances used to make objects.
Each material has properties like hardness, flexibility, and transparency.
We choose materials based on the job they need to do.
Natural materials come from nature; synthetic materials are made by humans.

slides.inSimpleWords: Everything is made of a material. Scientists and engineers choose the right material for each job!

slides.title: Your Turn: Classify Materials at Home
slides.storyContext: Look at 8-10 objects in your home. For each one, write: 1) What is it made of? 2) Is it natural or synthetic? 3) Why was this material chosen for this object?

example.problem: A pencil. What is it made of? Why?
example.solution: Pencil: wooden body (natural, hard, can be sharpened), graphite inside (synthetic mineral, leaves mark on paper), metal band (holds eraser), rubber eraser (synthetic, can erase pencil marks). Each part was chosen for its specific job!

slides.inSimpleWords: Be a material detective! Notice what things are made from and why.

subject: Science
title: Sarthak's Temperature Mystery: Hot, Cold, and In-Between
hook: A boy learns that temperature is not just 'hot' or 'cold'—it's a precise measurement of how fast tiny atoms are moving.

characters.name: Sarthak
characters.role: curious student investigating heat and cold

characters.name: Mother
characters.role: uses temperature in cooking and health

characters.name: Doctor Uncle
characters.role: teaches about body temperature and thermometers

slides.title: Temperature and its Measurement
slides.storyContext: Sarthak wakes up with a fever. His mother says, 'I need to check your temperature.' She uses a thermometer and says, '38°C—a mild fever.' Sarthak wonders: 'What is temperature? How does this thin tube know?'

slides.title: What is Temperature Really?
slides.storyContext: Doctor Uncle explains: 'Temperature measures how fast atoms and molecules are moving inside something. In hot water, atoms jiggle very fast. In cold water, they move slowly. A thermometer measures this jiggling motion as degrees.' Sarthak realizes: 'Temperature is like the speed of atoms!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature measures how fast atoms move. Hot things have fast-moving atoms; cold things have slow-moving atoms.

slides.title: Understanding Temperature vs. Heat

points.label: Temperature
points.text: A measurement of how fast atoms/molecules move. Measured in °C (Celsius), °F (Fahrenheit), or K (Kelvin).

points.label: Heat
points.text: Energy that flows from a hot object to a cold object. Heat always moves from hot to cold.
They are different! A cup of hot tea has higher temperature than a swimming pool, but the pool has more total heat energy because it's much bigger.

example.problem: A cup of boiling water (100°C) and a swimming pool of warm water (30°C). Which has higher temperature? Which has more heat?
example.solution: The cup has higher temperature (100°C > 30°C). But the pool has more total heat because it's much larger. Heat depends on both temperature AND the amount of substance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature is how hot or cold something is. Heat is energy moving from hot to cold.

slides.title: Temperature Scales and Their Uses

points.label: Celsius (°C)
points.text: Most common in India and science. Water freezes at 0°C, boils at 100°C. Body temperature is about 37°C.

points.label: Fahrenheit (°F)
points.text: Used in some countries. Water freezes at 32°F, boils at 212°F.

points.label: Kelvin (K)
points.text: Used in physics and science. Absolute zero = 0 K (nothing can be colder).

example.problem: Normal body temperature is 37°C. What is it in Fahrenheit?

slides.inSimpleWords: Celsius is used in India. Fahrenheit is used in other countries. They measure the same thing differently.

slides.title: Thermometers: How They Work

points.label: Liquid thermometer (mercury or alcohol)
points.text: Liquid expands when hot, contracts when cold. The column height shows temperature.

points.label: Digital thermometer
points.text: Uses an electronic sensor to measure temperature and displays it as a number.

points.label: How to read
points.text: Place the bulb (or sensor) in contact with the substance for 1-2 minutes. Read the number at eye level.

example.problem: A thermometer is half in hot water and half in air. Will it give the correct temperature of the water?
example.solution: No! The part in air will cool down, giving an incorrect reading. The entire bulb must be submerged in the substance being measured for accuracy.

slides.inSimpleWords: A thermometer measures temperature by sensing how much a liquid expands or using an electronic sensor.

slides.title: Measuring Temperature in Real Life

points.label: Body temperature
points.text: Healthy: 37°C (98.6°F). Fever: above 38°C. Hypothermia: below 35°C.

points.label: Cooking
points.text: Water boils at 100°C. Milk boils at 110°C. Ideal cooking temperatures vary.

points.label: Weather
points.text: India: summer heat can reach 45°C+; winter cold can drop to 5°C. Monitor temperatures for health and comfort.

points.label: Storage
points.text: Refrigerator: 4°C (keeps food fresh). Freezer: -18°C (preserves food for months).

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature is important in health, cooking, and keeping things fresh.

slides.title: Sarthak's Temperature Experiments
slides.storyContext: Sarthak measures temperature in different situations.

example.problem: Sarthak measures: 1) Room temperature: 25°C. 2) A cup of tea: 65°C. 3) Ice cube: -5°C (inside freezer). 4) His body: 37°C. Order these from coldest to hottest.
example.solution: Coldest to hottest: Ice cube (-5°C) < Room (25°C) < Body (37°C) < Tea (65°C). Cold objects cool down to room temperature over time, and hot objects cool down too. Eventually, everything reaches equilibrium!

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature is always changing. Hot things cool down, and cold things warm up until they match their environment.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Temperature measures how fast atoms and molecules move.
Heat is energy that flows from hot to cold objects.
Celsius scale: water freezes at 0°C, boils at 100°C. Body temperature is 37°C.
Thermometers measure temperature using liquid expansion or electronic sensors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature is everywhere in your life—in your health, food, weather, and environment. Measure it carefully!

image.alt: What We Learned — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Your Turn: Measure Temperatures Around You
slides.storyContext: Use a thermometer to measure temperature in different places at home for one day. Track: room temperature in morning and evening, water from the tap (hot and cold), food after cooking, your body temperature, and outdoor temperature.

example.problem: You measure: Morning room = 22°C, Evening room = 28°C, Tap water (cold) = 15°C, Tap water (hot) = 45°C, Cooked rice = 60°C, Body = 37°C, Outdoor = 35°C. What do you notice?
example.solution: Room temperature changes with the day (hotter in evening). Hot tap water is much warmer than cold. Cooked food is hot but cools down. Body stays constant at 37°C (unless sick). Outdoor is warmest. This shows that temperature varies a lot in your environment!

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure temperatures around you. You'll see how much they change throughout the day!
